VIDEO INTRODUCTION: On May 4th, 2026, the most powerful politician in South India — M. K. Stalin — walked into a polling booth in Chennai. He had been an MLA since 1989, was the sitting Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu, and came from a political dynasty that had ruled the state on and off for nearly 60 years through the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam. He voted in Kolathur, a seat he had won three times in a row. But by evening, Stalin had lost his own constituency — defeated by a man who had never held public office and had launched his party just two years earlier: Joseph Vijay.
His victory wasn’t just personal; it shattered a political duopoly that had dominated the state since 1967. For nearly six decades, power in Tamil Nadu had alternated between only two parties — the DMK and the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam. By 2026, both had begun to look strikingly similar in ideology, welfare politics, and corruption allegations. Challenging this entrenched system required something extraordinary — something that, in modern Tamil history, only one man had achieved before: M. G. Ramachandran.
MGR, a film superstar, launched his party and became Chief Minister within three years in 1977 with 33.5% of the vote — a record that stood untouched for nearly five decades. On May 4th, 2026, Joseph Vijay surpassed it, securing 35% of the vote and winning 108 out of 234 seats, becoming the single largest political force in Tamil Nadu’s history. The real question now is simple: how did a political outsider walk in and dismantle a 60-year-old duopoly in his very first election?

entry.title: Your Brain Hides 99.99% Reality | Ft. Nir Eyal

media:group.media:title: Your Brain Hides 99.99% Reality | Ft. Nir Eyal
media:group.media:description:
What if everything you see isn’t actually real?
In this podcast, Nir Eyal (Former Stanford professor & New York Times best selling author) reveals a mind-blowing truth about how our brain works. At any moment, your brain is processing around 11 million bits of information, but your conscious mind can only handle about 50 bits per second. That means what you call “reality” is just a tiny fraction of what actually exists. Your brain filters everything else and shows you a limited version of the world, creating a kind of simulation based on your attention.

media:group.media:title: What Diet Coke Paradox tells you about Indian Economy?
media:group.media:description:

⭐️ Think School’s flagship Communication course with live doubt sessions : https://thethinkschool.com/sp/communication-masterclass/
VIDEO INTRODUCTION: Over the past few weeks, Diet Coke has quietly disappeared from shelves across India, and Gen Z has been freaking out. When I tried to find out why, the answer sounded absurd: an “aluminium shortage.” That makes no sense on the surface. India is the world’s second-largest aluminium producer, with enough high-quality bauxite reserves to last roughly 350 years and some of the lowest labour costs globally. On paper, India should be the Saudi Arabia of aluminium.
But this isn’t just about soft-drink cans. The same pattern repeats across industries. We’re called the “pharmacy of the world,” yet we import around 70% of our active pharmaceutical ingredients from China. We are one of the largest producers of iron ore, yet we import specialty steel for our own bullet trains. We are the fourth-largest producer of rare earths, yet we don’t have a single commercial-scale rare-earth magnet factory.
This paradox exposes a deeper weakness in India’s growth story. Why are we importing aluminium cans from Sri Lanka when we have centuries’ worth of aluminium reserves? And more importantly, how is the government led by Narendra Modi supposed to fix this structural problem?
